passage: “Come sit, Gudiya, and I'll tell you about the bus-route marches of my school days. I'm Rekha, your Dadi. I was fifteen, and half the town was marching for a new school bus. Asif from my class kept saying, ‘Only cowards stay home.’ That stung. But I sat on the veranda and counted on my fingers. March: I'm small, Papa won't allow it, and crowds get wild. Petition: forty signatures by Friday, easy. Letter to the councillor: one evening. Speaking at assembly: frightening, but the principal listens. Then I asked myself what I truly wanted. A bus. Not my face in a crowd photograph. So I did the petition and the assembly speech. Asif still grumbled that I had hidden. But in March the route was changed.”

qa.q: How many signatures did Rekha think she could collect by Friday?
qa.a: About forty, which she called easy.

qa.q: How did Rekha feel when Asif said only cowards stay home?
qa.a: It stung, so she felt hurt and pressured, but she still sat down to think it through.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Rekha's choice, and why did it work?
qa.a: Asking herself what she truly wanted, a bus and not a photograph in the crowd, showed that a petition and an assembly speech could reach that aim within her age and her father's limits.

qa.q: How might Asif have seen Rekha's choice?
qa.a: Asif grumbled that she had hidden, so Asif probably saw staying out of the march as playing safe, and may not have noticed that the petition and speech were lawful ways to get the same result.

grounding: A teen weighs a petition, a letter, an assembly speech and marching, and picks lawful options that fit age and risk.

passage:
The rally about the polluted lake in Bengaluru was on Saturday, and Preeti couldn't go: her grandmother was unwell, and she had to stay home with her all weekend. Her friend Omkar was going. "You'll miss it," he said on the phone.

Preeti sat by her grandmother's bed with a notebook. She wanted to do something real. She listed the choices. The rally itself: not possible, and crowds aren't her thing anyway. An online petition: quick, but would anyone read it? A letter to the local ward councillor: slow, but official. Speaking at the school's Monday assembly forum: she'd get three minutes. A poster about the lake for her housing society: easy, and people would see it daily.

She chose two. That evening she wrote the letter to the councillor, with photos of the foam on the lake. On Monday, at the forum, she read it aloud and asked classmates to sign it.

qa.q: Why couldn't Preeti go to the rally?
qa.a: Her grandmother was unwell, and she had to stay home with her all weekend.

qa.q: How did Preeti feel when Omkar said she would miss it?
qa.a: She likely felt left out and frustrated, which pushed her to look for a real way to contribute from home.

qa.q: Which of Preeti's choices might have the most effect, and why?
qa.a: The letter to the ward councillor may matter most, because it goes to someone with power over the lake, and the forum reading added classmates' signatures.

qa.q: How might Omkar see Preeti's letter when he hears about it?
qa.a: Omkar may feel impressed and encouraged, seeing that she found a way to help the same cause without being at the rally.

grounding: Shows a teen, kept home by a family need, weighing a petition, a letter to a representative, a school forum and posters, and choosing ways that fit age and risk.

passage:
Kamal had seen the notice on the colony board in Lucknow: a road-blockade on Sunday to protest the closure of the public library branch. He loved that library. He'd grown up in its children's corner.

But a blockade on the main road, at fifteen? His friend Jatin, who was going, said, "It's the only way they'll listen."

Kamal wasn't sure. That night he opened a notebook and listed other ways. Sign the online petition: easy, but lots of people sign and forget. Write to the MLA's office: slow, but it goes on record. Ask to speak at the Residents' Welfare Association meeting: they were meeting Friday. Collect memories from old library members and put them on a board outside.

He chose the letter and the RWA meeting. On Friday he read his letter aloud to thirty adults, and the RWA voted to send it with their own stamp.

qa.q: When was the Residents' Welfare Association meeting?
How did Kamal feel about the blockade?
qa.a: Kamal felt unsure and uneasy, caring about the library but wary of a road-blockade at fifteen.

qa.q: What else could Kamal do if the letter gets no reply?
qa.a: He could follow up with the RWA and collect the memories board as planned, keeping pressure up in lawful ways.

qa.q: How might Jatin see Kamal's choice?
qa.a: Jatin might feel he was being too cautious at first, but seeing the RWA back the letter may show him it also worked.

grounding: Shows a teen weighing a petition, a letter to a representative, a residents' forum and awareness boards, and picking ways that fit his age and risk.
